Abel Ferro, the tuner, reached the Pellam Street hall on a snowy Thursday, two days before Lise Marrow's recital. Lise, the town's best young pianist, said the old upright had been sounding wrong all winter, dull in the bass and quick to slip. Nell Ostrand, the hall's manager, had sent for him, and Edith Garvey, the hall's benefactor, had offered the committee the gift of a new piano if the old one proved worn out.

Tobias Rusk, Abel's old teacher, had first seen the crack thirty years ago and written it into his notebook: 'hairline split in the board, two inches, watch it.' In March Lise pointed it out again, Owen Dorran, the caretaker, measured it, and Nell passed the news to Mrs. Garvey. Rusk had always tuned this piano a shade below standard pitch, and Abel had kept to that pitch each October since Rusk died, at the committee's expense. Lise had learned on it.

The piano stood where it always had, at the far end from the stove. Abel looked for a broken string, ready to fit a new one, and found every string sound. But the split now ran the width of the board, and a tuning held there for a week at most. It struck Abel, running his thumb along it, that Rusk had known from the start how this would end. He tuned it anyway, note by note, at Rusk's pitch, for one more evening.

'Will it be ready for Saturday?' Nell asked. Abel kept his hand on the lid. 'For Saturday, yes. You should have heard this bass twenty years ago. It rang like a bell, and the whole hall hummed with it. That's gone now, and tuning won't fetch it back.' He pressed the low C once and listened to it fade.

On Saturday Lise went through her whole programme without a sour note, and the old piano held for one evening more. Mrs. Garvey's new piano was to arrive on Monday, and Owen had cleared a space for it. Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring short and dull on the final chord.

passage:
For forty-six summers a carousel turned on Larkmoor common, its twenty-four horses carved in 1912 by Josiah Fenn. When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.

Nora Quill had ridden those horses as a girl. In 1991, newly retired from the post office, she found the auction ledger among some council papers, and she spent that first winter reading everything she could find on repairing old band organs. The families who had bought the horses were easy to trace, and most agreed to send them home. The first horse she brought home had stood in the entrance hall of a school. After it came horses from a saddler's shop, a chapel basement, an ivied garden and a hotel lobby in Brannock, until every horse but one was back within the year.

Where the carousel would stand was another matter. Nora wanted it on the common; the council wanted the station yard. The dispute ran through eleven meetings and two winters, until a councillor raised the matter of the common's drains and the yard won by one vote. By then the town raffle, its tickets printed with a photograph taken in 1923 of the carousel in full swing, had sold out in a week, and the money paid for the restoration. The band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows, and the original colours showed plainly under later paint.

That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction. Hal and Nora had sung side by side in the chapel choir for twenty years. When she asked for the grey, he told her she could have it if she could catch it, and led her to a stall where the wooden horse stood between his two real ones, wearing a halter, a bucket of oats at its feet. He hitched up the trailer that afternoon.

The carousel turned again in the station yard in July 1996. Nora spent the afternoon ticking off lot numbers in the ledger as children climbed on.

passage:
For sixteen summers Dr. Hana Vell has counted the sand beetles of Orsk Spit, pale hunters the size of a thumbnail. They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

Much had changed on the spit that year. Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence that ran the whole length of the dune foot, its slats a hand's width apart. A March storm tore away the dune's seaward face and much of the old crest with it. In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir, and visitors began to stray from it onto the dune. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass.

For a week Arkin walked the dune at dawn counting bootprints, and found nearly all of them in the north hollow, a kilometre past the last trap. On the walk back he saw that the middle traps sat in loose sand on the landward slope. Vell's notebooks held a sketch of the dune drawn the day the traps were first set, and laid beside the dune as it now stood, it showed the crest twelve metres further inland. The beetles had moved with it, burrowing where the traps were no longer.

Arkin brought the sketch to Vell's desk and asked whether they should tell the park. Vell said he would be the one to tell them, and slid the season report across the desk. She had crossed out her own name on its first page and written his above it.

Vell moved the traps up onto the new crest. This July the count was seven hundred and eighty; last year's figure, she now writes, measured the traps rather than the beetles.
